language_wrapper: In a math contest, consider the set of consecutive positive integers {start, start+1, ..., n}. A subset is said to have the acute-triangle property if it contains three distinct elements that can serve as side lengths of an acute triangle (equivalently, for some x<y<z in the subset, x^2 + y^2 > z^2). Determine the largest possible value of n such that every subset of size {subset_size} drawn from {start, start+1, ..., n} has the acute-triangle property.
hardness_rationale: The seed problem uses the triangle inequality a+b>c and reduces to controlling triangle-free subsets via a Fibonacci-like superincreasing sequence starting from the smallest elements. Our augmentation strengthens the requirement to acute triangles, which necessitates x^2 + y^2 > z^2. Avoiding acute triangles imposes a Pythagorean superincreasing constraint t_k >= ceil(sqrt(t_{k-1}^2 + t_{k-2}^2)), which grows faster and is more delicate to analyze. The extremal construction and proof demand handling quadratic growth, leveraging monotonicity of sums of squares, and a careful greedy extremal argument. The parameterized subset size further complicates the threshold analysis, making guessing impossible and requiring a structured recurrence-based proof.
notes: Proof sketch of correctness: Let S be any subset of {start, start+1, ..., n} with elements t_1 < t_2 < ... < t_m. A triple (t_i, t_j, t_k) with i<j<k forms an acute triangle iff t_i^2 + t_j^2 > t_k^2. Among all choices with fixed k, the largest left-hand side occurs for (i,j) = (k-2, k-1) since the sequence is increasing; thus the most restrictive non-acute condition is t_{k-2}^2 + t_{k-1}^2 <= t_k^2. Consequently, a subset is acute-free iff for all k>=3, t_k >= ceil(sqrt(t_{k-1}^2 + t_{k-2}^2)). The extremal way to pack as many elements as possible below an upper bound n, while remaining acute-free, is to take the greedy sequence r_1 = start, r_2 = start+1, r_k = ceil(sqrt(r_{k-1}^2 + r_{k-2}^2)). This sequence minimizes each r_k subject to the constraints, by induction using monotonicity of sqrt and nondecreasingness of the terms. Therefore, an acute-free subset of size s exists in {start, ..., n} iff n >= r_s. It follows that the largest n forcing every s-element subset to contain an acute triangle is r_s - 1. The verifier certifies this by constructing the extremal greedy sequence at n = r_s and confirming it fits, and that it cannot fit at n = r_s - 1, ensuring tightness.
source_question: A set of positive numbers has the $triangle~property$ if it has three distinct elements that are the lengths of the sides of a triangle whose area is positive. Consider sets $\{4, 5, 6, \ldots, n\}$ of consecutive positive integers, all of whose ten-element subsets have the triangle property. What is the largest possible value of $n$ ?
